claim: Difficulty in matchstick arithmetic follows how much of the default frame must be changed: value change (A) is easiest, operator change (B) and tautology change (C) are hard. Solution rates and times followed the predicted order in several labs.
agent_test: Build a task family with graded constraint depth (drop a value rule, an operator rule, a whole-structure rule). Check that plain-model failure rises with depth; this is the base for the S6 impasse probe.

claim: Tight chunks (single units such as X or a stroke) are harder to take apart than loose chunks (composite numerals or radicals). Decomposition cost, not regrouping cost, drives the difficulty.
agent_test: Items where the key move needs splitting a unit the prompt presents as atomic (a token, a number, a word). Compare plain vs a prompt that asks to list the parts of each unit first, at equal tokens.

claim: Relaxing a constraint is causally separable from decomposing a chunk. Solving tautological Type C first removed the Type C difficulty (61% to 100% in Block 2); Type D (chunk) initial solution rate was unaffected. In solution time Type D did improve after exposure (p<.01), so the separation is partial. Gap search: the Type D time gain is probably practice, because the tautology set included a tautological Type D item that also needs chunk decomposition (d01). The separation therefore holds for rates and is not undone by times.
agent_test: Cue-only test: give a drop-constraint hint to constraint items and a decompose hint to chunk items; check each hint helps only its own type (b22, abstract only, reports this in humans). Run on LLM items of both types at equal tokens.

claim: Transfer between insight problems follows representational change, not surface similarity. Same problem, same numerals or different problem gave almost no similarity effect on solution frequency.
agent_test: Store the relaxed constraint as a rule, not the solved item. Test retrieval by constraint type against retrieval by surface similarity.

claim: Eye tracking: fixations are longer on hard problems and grow over time; attention starts on values and avoids operator signs; solvers of the operator problem shift to the operator late. This matches a wrong initial representation then a late re-representation.
agent_test: Treat early attention as a diagnostic: log which parts of the problem the model quotes or acts on in its first attempt. If it never touches the critical element, fire O6 or O4 rather than more sampling.

claim: The shift to the critical element is sudden near the end of solving, not gradual (change-point analysis gives about the 90 percent time bin), supporting a discrete re-representation event.
agent_test: One reanalysis of one dataset (N=61), and a13 and b16 are the same paper. Look in the model's attempt sequence for a step change in which elements it uses before a correct answer; do not use this to time an operator. Gap search: no second dataset found; Danek et al. 2016 add that Aha falls as constraints stack, so suddenness is weaker on multi-constraint items.

claim: Fixation duration and early element bias separate hard from easy problems but do not separate eventual solvers from non-solvers early on; only the late shift does.
agent_test: Do not predict solving from one length or confidence feature. Use the impasse detector plus a failed check (G1).

claim: Dropping a constraint in one place is not enough: car-park non-solvers moved the taxi but put it back. Solvers also noticed the new area that the move opened.
agent_test: After O4 produces a relaxed problem, require the agent to state what the relaxation now allows and test it by code. Compare with O4 followed by free continuation.

claim: Heuristic hill-climbing does not explain matchstick difficulty; the required degree of constraint relaxation does. Solvers mostly try value moves first (60.9% of 509 equations) and operator moves least (16.6%). The progress-monitoring account makes different lookahead predictions that were only partly met.
agent_test: Vary move-count lookahead and constraint depth separately in an agent task and see which predicts failure. Link: progress monitoring theory subfield.

claim: Prior success with same-type problems can create a mental set. Repeating non-insight set problems did not hurt later insight problems; repeating insight set problems helped or hurt by type.
agent_test: Check whether a failed first frame carried inside one context hurts later items. Test by clearing history before a re-attempt at equal tokens. Gap search: LLM evidence now points one way. Failed early answers persist in context (d09: unreliability +112%) and the model corrects the same error far less when it is its own output (d10: 64.5% blind spot).

claim: Hands-on or interactive material does not reliably raise insight. The 2011 interactive effect failed to replicate in three experiments (participants rarely moved sticks); a 2026 study found no gain from physical interaction on a pencil match problem.
agent_test: Not an agent lever. Do not add a build-it-physically step. The one reported benefit (a photo of real overlapping sticks, 47% to 79%, b11) is a perception change, possibly a diagram operator; a19 is second hand.

claim: Cathodal stimulation that dampens left prefrontal rule use raised solving only on the two-constraint Type C problem (32% vs 5% and 5%, N=60).
agent_test: Analogy only: loosening rule enforcement helps when many rules must go. Test lower rule-priority prompts only on high-depth items; expect harm elsewhere.

claim: Cuing the right mechanism helps only the matching problem type; cuing both at once does not add benefit and sometimes lowers solving (Miller, Wiley, Ohlsson 2025, full abstract read; sample sizes unavailable). In Study 2 the constraint-relaxation cue did not raise relaxation solutions at all.
agent_test: Abstract only. Route by diagnosis: pick O4 or O6 per impasse signal, never apply both prompts at once. Test routed vs combined prompts at equal tokens.

claim: People better at repairing a wrong early reading of an ambiguous sentence solve more anagram and creative problems beyond working memory and fluid intelligence (partial r=0.41, Exp 1 N=85).
agent_test: Individual-difference result, not a prompt result. A garden-path check item could be a cheap model-level reanalysis probe.

claim: Misleading cues cause fixation in people: false hints lower anagram success and practising the wrong movement pattern lowers nine-dot success (37.5% vs 78.1%).
agent_test: Seed the first context with a wrong frame and measure whether a re-representation operator escapes it versus plain resampling at equal tokens.

claim: LLMs fall far below humans on riddle and lateral-thinking tasks that need a default assumption dropped (NazoNazo 17.6% vs human 52.9%; BrainTeaser human about 92% vs model 53-63%; Only Connect, MathSticks, rebus, M-ARC show gaps).
agent_test: Use these as the evaluation family for the representation step: BrainTeaser sentence set and a MathSticks sample, plain vs scaffold at equal tokens.

claim: The main reasoning-model failure on insight-like riddles is verification: the right answer is generated but not endorsed (5.2% to 39.3% of wrong answers contained the gold answer in the thought log). Added: more than 70% of wrong o1-like responses hold a correct thought (d11), and hidden states encode answer correctness (AUC above 0.7, d12), so the model often knows more than it endorses.
agent_test: Keep every candidate generated during search and rank them by an external check, not by the final-answer decision. Compare final-answer-only vs all-candidates-checked at equal tokens.

claim: Spontaneous mid-reasoning aha shifts are rare (about 6.3% of traces) and usually go with lower accuracy; they do not grow with RL training. Model 'Oh!' language is not evidence of insight.
agent_test: Never treat insight words in output as a signal to accept or switch. Trigger shifts from checks (G1, G10).

claim: An external reconsideration cue helps strongly on math (32.2% to 40.6%, +8.4 points) but barely on cryptic crosswords (+0.45) and about zero on Rush Hour. Gain is larger when first-pass entropy is high.
agent_test: Small GRPO-tuned models and a generic 'wait' cue. Compare a generic reconsider cue vs a specific O4/O6 cue gated on a failed check, on one insight set and one math set.

claim: Later reflection in a reasoning trace is mostly confirmation: over 90% keep the first candidate and wrong-to-right changes are mostly under 2%. Cutting reflection after the first candidate saves 24.5% of tokens for under 3% accuracy loss.
agent_test: Test a cap after the first candidate vs free reflection at equal tokens, then spend the saved tokens on a representation operator.

claim: Restating the problem at a more abstract level (step-back) or giving structure-matched examples improves hard reasoning: step-back +7 to +11 points on PaLM-2L physics and chemistry, +25 on TimeQA; it fixes 20.5% of baseline errors but breaks 11.9%.
agent_test: Test step-back as O2/O6 on insight sets. Report the break rate (new errors), not only the fix rate.

claim: LLM-assisted problem reframing for designers did not beat control in a large human study (N=280). This agrees with the schema note that O8 reframing is null in one large test.
agent_test: Abstract-level only; keep O8 behind a code-visible failing output (G2).

claim: No one has run Knoblich's matchstick types A to D with tightness labels on language models. MathSticks (2025) gives only a proxy: strong models score 8 to 14 points lower on text puzzles that need the sign changed (o3 51.45 vs 65.19; Gemini-2.5-Pro 38.91 vs 49.09; o4-mini 21.15 vs 26.95). The digit-edit bias is asserted without per-edit counts.
agent_test: Run a small paired test: matchstick items by constraint depth, plain vs O4/O6 routed, at equal tokens, reported per type. Hand the model the unit to split as characters or digits by code; tokenization decides which chunks are tight (d08).

claim: Goal relaxation by an LLM with a classical planner checking feasibility lifts planning success (+52%), but this is a snippet-level report.
agent_test: Check the source before use. The design (relax, then verify by code) matches the schema.

claim: No study compares a prompt that names the constraint or unit to change with a generic reconsider cue on LLM insight items. Gap 1 is open. The closest results are human: targeted cues work only on matching items (d03), and a worked prototype may beat plain instructions (d04, snippet only).
agent_test: Run the missing test: generic Wait-style cue, named-constraint cue, named-unit cue, and a neutral resample, all at equal tokens, on constraint items and chunk items.

claim: A generic correction marker is a strong cheap baseline: appending Wait cuts the self-correction blind spot by 89.3% in 14 non-reasoning models. Any named-operator cue must beat this, not only a no-cue control.
agent_test: Include Wait-style and C1-style generic cues as arms in the O4/O6 test. Report net gain including new errors.

claim: Output-only impasse detection is partial. Thought-switch rate separates wrong from right (418% more switches in wrong responses), first-pass entropy predicts cue benefit, and answer stability marks when more compute is idle. None of these is tested as a detector of fixation, and stable-and-wrong looks the same as stable-and-right.
agent_test: Do not gate O4/O6 on an output statistic alone. Gate on a code-visible failure (verifier fails, repeated candidate rejected), and log the statistic to measure its false-trigger rate.

claim: Failed-frame carry-over inside one LLM context is supported indirectly: models rely on early wrong answers and do not recover, and correct the same error far less when it is their own output. A clean-context restatement is the better default than stacking another turn. Not yet tested on insight items.
agent_test: Compare: continue in context, continue with failed attempt relabelled as a user draft, and fresh context with a code-written summary of what failed. Equal tokens.

claim: Chunk tightness is tokenizer dependent for models: whole-word replacement is easy, character insertion and deletion are hard (GPT-4 F .368 and .277 vs human 1.0). Operator-change matchstick items are harder than digit-only ones for strong models.
agent_test: Give O6 a code-side splitter that exposes characters or digits. Test per-type with matchstick items grouped by edit type.

claim: Re-representing an ARC-type input by code (object-based encoding) nearly doubled GPT-4's solved tasks (13 of 50 baseline). Model-side reframing has no matching evidence on ARC. Abstract-level only.
agent_test: On ARC items try the code-side object re-encoding before any reframe prompt; measure net fix and break rate per task class.

claim: Selection and verification, not generation, may explain a large share of LLM failures: over 70% of wrong responses contain a correct thought and models encode correctness in hidden states without using it. This argues for code-side ranking of all candidates (G5) before adding a representation operator.
agent_test: On each target set, count wrong answers whose log holds the gold answer. If that share is large, fix selection first.

claim: Ohlsson's 2011 redistribution account remains unverified: only the chapter opening (Raisins in the Dough principle and three explanatory tasks) is public, and the 1992 account was not found. No operational use for LLM memory retrieval can be claimed.
agent_test: Needs library access to the chapter. Until then keep a21 as unverified.
